evidence.title: multipart: add per-part/file size guards, content-type validation, and OpenAI-compat field mapping
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: customers using the OpenAI-compatibility layer and the tool/function-calling endpoints were able to upload large multipart payloads and malformed parts which caused OOMs and destabilized streaming. This PR centralizes multipart validation into the API gateway handler and adds explicit per-part and total payload limits, content-type sniffing, and dual-field support for OpenAI-compat clients (accept both 'file' and 'files' form fields). The change is intentionally conservative: we validate before handing off to the streaming runtime so we can guarantee early rejection and deterministic error responses instead of mid-stream failures. Implementation highlights: 1) api/handlers/multipart_handler.py implements a two-pass scan: fast header-only pass to enforce per-part size and type heuristics, followed by a streaming handoff that preserves the original stream for allowed parts. 2) Introduced config flags (env) for PART_MAX_BYTES and MULTIPART_TOTAL_MAX_BYTES with sane defaults (10MB per part, 50MB total) and runtime metrics emitted for rejected uploads. 3) Content-type safety: we perform lightweight sniffing (magic bytes + declared header) to avoid accepting text/plain labeled binary blobs; for non-whitelisted types we respond 415 with structured error payload. 4) OpenAI-compat: map legacy form names and accept arrays and singletons to reduce client breakage. 5) Added unit and integration tests covering edge cases and a small e2e run that exercises the streaming generation + tool-call with an uploaded schema file. Checklist: - [x] Implement server-side validation and env flags - [x] Add metrics and structured error responses - [x] Add unit tests and integration e2e - [x] Update docs/compatibility and API reference - [x] Add a hotfix note for incident INT-4421 in changelog

evidence.title: Validate multipart boundaries and enforce file-size/content-type limits on OpenAI-compat tool/file endpoints
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: several incidents and flaky E2E runs showed that tool/file uploads to the OpenAI-compat endpoints could hang or be accepted with malformed boundaries or incorrect content-type headers, leading to streaming stalls and memory spikes on private deployments. This PR tightens validation for multipart/form-data and chunked transfer uploads, adds enforcement of default file-size limits, and surfaces explicit compatibility-layer error codes so downstream SDKs and clients can handle rejections cleanly. Summary of changes: - Add a multipart boundary presence and consistency check early in request parsing; reject requests missing a boundary with 422 MALFORMED_MULTIPART. - Enforce Content-Type whitelist for tool/file payloads (application/octet-stream, image/*, text/*, application/json, multipart/form-data). Requests with disallowed content-types now return 400 INVALID_CONTENT_TYPE. - Introduce Content-Length and chunked streaming guards. For chunked uploads we now apply per-chunk size ceiling and an aggregate max (default 25MB) and return 413 FILE_TOO_LARGE when exceeded. Limit is configurable via service config and Dedicated/Private can override per-tenant. - Update the OpenAI-compat adapter to normalize incoming form-data to internal file objects, while preserving streaming semantics. Old behavior accepted missing boundary on some clients; new behavior rejects those requests but includes a compatibility hint header (X-Compat-Error) to aid callers. - Add a small in-memory streaming parser for boundary edge-cases to avoid allocating large buffers when boundaries come in split TCP frames. - Bake in tests: unit tests for malformed boundary paths, integration tests with chunked transfer encoding (nginx-style split chunks), e2e test that runs against the compatibility layer. - Documentation: api changelog + compatibility notes and SDK test expectations. Risk & rollout: - Backwards compatible at the protocol level for well-formed clients; some malformed clients will be rejected. To soften rollout we emit the X-Compat-Error hints and a telemetry metric (compat.multipart.reject_count) for 2 weeks before flipping enforcement in some private installs where customers asked for a grace period. - Default file-size cap is conservative (25MB); customers can configure via config.service.file_upload.max_size_bytes. Related: ENG-4132 (multipart resilience), PM-291 (compat ergonomics).

evidence.title: add multipart/form-data handling, strict content-type validation, and payload limit enforcement for API tool/file inputs
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout. Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md -

evidence.title: Enforce MIME sniffing and chunking limits for tool/file uploads (OpenAI-compat layer)
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: Tool integrations and file attachments coming through the OpenAI-compatibility proxy were accepting overly permissive Content-Type headers and arbitrarily large streaming chunks which caused downstream model handlers to OOM or misclassify payloads. This PR adds deterministic MIME sniffing, per-tool attachment quotas, and streaming chunk size enforcement at the proxy layer so tool authors and user clients get immediate, deterministic rejections instead of opaque runtime errors.

What this changes: - Add a MIME sniffing pass for multipart and single-part uploads that normalizes Content-Type to a safe set and rejects unknown/binary blobs when a tool opts into textual input only. - Implement per-tool max_upload_bytes and max_chunks settings surfaced through the tools registry; defaults applied when not configured. - Enforce max_chunk_bytes for streaming/transfer-encoding style uploads so a single chunk cannot exceed safety limits. - Map legacy OpenAI style headers ("OpenAI-File-Name", "openai-content-type") into our normalized metadata to keep compatibility with existing clients. - Return structured JSON error payloads compatible with OpenAI-compat error shapes (error.code, error.message, error.type) so SDKs can handle programmatic failures. - Add unit and integration tests that exercise multipart boundaries, chunked streams, and header-based compatibility fallbacks.

Checklist: - [x] Add MIME sniffing implementation and canonicalizer in api/proxy/upload_validator.go - [x] Add per-tool config + defaults in services/tools/registry - [x] Add streaming chunk enforcement in streaming/handler.go - [x] Preserve OpenAI compatibility headers and map to internal metadata - [x] Add tests for multipart streaming, single-part file uploads, and header fallbacks - [x] Update docs: redwood-docs/api/file-uploads.md

Compatibility notes: This change preserves behavioral compatibility for existing clients that set Content-Type correctly. Clients relying on implicit server-side assumptions (e.g. sending mixed binary/text under text/plain) will now receive a structured 400 with guidance. Ops: rollout is safe behind a feature flag (features.validate_tool_uploads). Default is off for 48 hours to allow canary release, then on cluster-wide by default.

References: Linear ENG-7382 (upload hardening), incident SUP-4127 (tool-run OOM on binary attachment), and a related follow-up PR will add per-tenant overrides for enterprise Private deployments.

Notes on testing and observations: integration tests found a tokenizer mismatch when content-type was incorrectly marked as "text/plain; charset=utf-16"; MIME canonicalizer now strips charset and uses content sniffed encoding detection for tokenization. CI: one flaky streaming test needed a 200ms backoff retry; I renamed the test to reflect expected semantics.

evidence.title: streaming-backpressure-and-compat-layer-contenttype-guards-with-tool-payload-throttle
evidence.text:
description:
Motivation: Several recent incidents and internal customer reports highlighted two recurring issues: (1) multipart file uploads used by tool/function-calling flows could cause unbounded memory/queue growth when clients stream faster than worker throughput; (2) the OpenAI-compatibility layer did not consistently enforce content-type and structured-output size constraints which allowed oversized tool payloads to propagate to downstream runners. This PR introduces coordinated protections across the API entrypoint and compatibility shim to make streaming uploads more resilient and to place deterministic limits on tool/file payloads. Summary of changes: - Add streaming backpressure checks at the multipart parser level: per-connection in-flight byte quotas, configurable low/high watermarks, and early 413-style rejections when quotas are exceeded. This prevents request buffering at the gateway and gives predictable failure semantics for fast clients. - Introduce a "X-Tool-Payload-Quota" header that the compat layer will return in streaming responses for tool-calls; the header communicates server-allocated byte budget and remaining allowance so clients can adapt backoff behavior. - Implement server-side throttling for tool file payloads: if a tool upload exceeds its negotiated quota, the server will gracefully terminate the stream and emit structured diagnostics (JSON body with quota_used and limit). - Tighten content-type validation on the OpenAI compatibility endpoint: accept only a small whitelist (multipart/form-data, application/json, application/octet-stream) for attachments and reject ambiguous types (e.g., text/plain with non-UTF8). Also normalize and strip suspicious charset parameters. - Add structured-output size guard for function/tool-calls: the runtime will enforce a serialized size cap for tool responses when wired through the compat layer, with fallback policy support (truncate / error / partial-result). - Add tests (unit + integration) that simulate fast-producer slow-consumer streaming and verify quotas, header propagation, and diagnostic payloads. - Docs and changelog entries for the new headers and configuration knobs. Backwards compatibility: default quotas are conservative and can be raised by config; compat-layer behavior keeps response format stable and only adds the optional header. There is a brief note in CHANGELOG about a new rejected response shape for quota failures so customers can detect and surface them. See release_notes for details. Implementation notes: The backpressure implementation sits in the multipart parser middleware so it applies to both native API routes and the OpenAI-compat gateway. The quota enforcement is per-upload part and per-connection aggregated; we added metrics for quota_rejections, quota_bytes_consumed, and compat_header_emitted. We preferred early reject semantics to avoid head-of-line blocking in the request pipeline. Why this is different from earlier multipart commits: earlier PRs

description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when a browser client behind an enterprise reverse proxy (corporate NGN/inspect proxy) reconnects an SSE stream, the final JSON choice is sometimes split across two fragments and the stream ends with 4-6s of trailing silence before an EOF event. Impact: downstream application shows 'incomplete assistant response' and discards last sentence in 12% of reconnect events.

Impact: BrightChat AI's customer-facing chat widget is intermittently missing the last sentence after network blips, causing UX regressions for end-users. Several paid enterprise customers noticed degraded conversational quality.

Environment: prod traffic routed through customer's corporate proxy chain -> customer edge -> Redwood API Gateway -> serving runtime. Client SDK: web-sdk@1.8.2 (EventSource-based SSE).

Observed behavior: on reconnect, server emits resume event and then a sequence of data chunks. A JSON metadata chunk that includes 'finish_reason' sometimes arrives split (e.g., '{"choices":[{"text":"...","finish_reason":"' then 'length"}]}'), causing client JSON parse errors or partial choice rendering. Additionally, there is a multi-second gap (4-6s) of no data before final EOF event in a subset of sessions.

Expected behavior: resume and finalization messages should be emitted as complete JSON tokens and the stream should deliver EOF promptly (sub-second) after final content.

Steps to reproduce: 1) Use web-sdk@1.8.2 behind an enterprise transparent proxy that performs TLS inspection and connection pooling. 2) Initiate long streaming generation (approx 400-800 tokens) with SSE. 3) Simulate short network blip (TCP FIN then reconnect, or client re-establish EventSource). 4) Observe client-side partial JSON parse or silent gap before EOF.

Notes: Customer provided an HAR, tcpdump slices from their edge, and a minimal reproduction app. The problem is not consistently reproducible in staging where proxy chain is absent.

description:
Issue summary: Customer reports that when their corporate edge rewrites Streaming SSE to a long-poll fallback path, the last ~1-2 sentences of responses are consistently missing after a reconnect.

evidence.text:
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports that when a streaming SSE connection briefly drops during a TLS renegotiation event at the edge, the client receives a truncated final output: the last sentence or final punctuation is missing and no explicit end marker arrives. The server logs show the completion event emitted, but the client-side stream terminates early after reconnect.

Impact:
- Affects Inkling Health's production inference pipelines in eu-west.
- Partial outputs break downstream post-processing and fail schema validation for their clinical note ingestion (automated).
- Observed on ~3% of long-running streaming sessions during peak load windows.

Environment:
- prod (eu-west) behind vendor edge proxy (CloudEdge) + vendor CDN.
- Clients use SSE long-polling from browser and also a Node.js backend that implements reconnect/resume.
- Model: rw-instruct-large-v1, typical max_tokens ~1024, average response length ~600 tokens.

Steps to reproduce (customer-provided):
1) Start a long streaming generation from eu-west with prefix that yields a long final sentence.
2) Simulate TLS renegotiation at the edge by triggering a short RST/reconnect (they used their synthetic traffic tool to flip the client IP and trigger a rehandshake).
3) Observe returned stream on client: most of the time it resumes fine, but in a subset the final sentence is cut off and no terminal event arrives.

Expected behavior:
- Client should receive full streamed tokens including terminal metadata (choice completion). Reconnect/resume should either stitch output seamlessly or include an explicit end marker.

Actual behavior:
- Server emits completion and logs show terminal event for the request id, but the client sees an abrupt stop after an earlier chunk. No explicit "[DONE]" or terminal JSON arrives. Reconnect handshake shows success, but resumed stream never emits the missing trailing tokens.

Workaround (customer):
- Increase client-side post-reconnect polling window and re-request tail tokens using non-streaming completion API; this recovers text but adds latency and cost.

evidence.title: Data Access Certification & Retention Escrow — proposal
evidence.text:
Purpose and context:
This draft proposes a short-form contractual clause and operational runbook for (i) certification of data access events and (ii) a limited retention escrow (evidence escrow) tied to on-prem and private deployments of Redwood inference. Aim is to give customers a bounded way to obtain third-party-verifiable records for compliance/legal needs while minimizing long-term retention risk for Redwood.

Key objectives (design principles):
- Time-boxed: escrowed artifacts are retained only for a narrowly scoped period (default 90 days) unless the customer triggers a preservation request.
- Minimal content: store metadata/transactional logs and redacted payloads rather than full user content unless strictly required and mutually agreed.
- Verifiability: artifacts should be cryptographically stamped and accompanied by a tamper-evident manifest for independent audit.
- Operational controls: well-defined access request, approval workflow, and emergency suspension process.

Definitions (working):
- "Evidence Escrow Vault": a secured storage location (customer-managed S3-compatible or Redwood-hosted sealed store) where preserved artifacts are placed.
- "Certified Access Report (CAR)": a signed package including event metadata, cryptographic checksum(s), access-control snapshot, and operator attestations for a given time window.
- "Retention Window": the default period that artifacts are kept in the Evidence Escrow Vault (proposed: 90 days).
- "Preservation Trigger": an authenticated customer request (legal hold, litigation hold, regulatory inquiry) that extends retention for specified items.

Draft clause (contract language — short form):
1) Escrowed Artifacts. Vendor shall place, for the Retention Window, a copy of the artifacts specified in Schedule A ("Escrowed Artifacts") into the Evidence Escrow Vault. Escrowed Artifacts will be limited to: service logs, index-level metadata, access-control snapshots, and redacted request identifiers. evidence.text:
## Overview
The Interactive Latency Canvas is a single exploratory dashboard that allows SREs, Runtime, and product owners to compare latency distributions across **models** and **routes**, with an explicit decomposition between **streaming** and **blocking** (non-streaming) response modes.

This page is the implementation guide for:
- Required **metrics + trace attributes**
- Cardinality controls (what we will/won’t tag)
- Dashboard panel requirements
- Alerting recipes and validation steps

## Goals
1. Surface p50/p95/p99 latency by **model_version** and **route_name**, with a toggle for **io_mode = streaming|blocking**.
2. Enable cohort-based comparisons:
   - prompt length bucket (token-based)
   - request shape bucket (short/medium/long *completion length*)
   - KV-cache hit/miss
   - client_region
3. Provide explanatory overlays:
   - KV-cache hit rate
   - batch size distribution
   - stream “first token” latency
   - kernel variant selection frequency
4. Link directly to pre-sampled traces (high p99, KV-miss, fallback) for root-cause drilldown.
5. Provide alerting templates for **streaming regressions** (p95/p99) and **first-token latency** regressions.

## Non-goals (explicitly out of scope)
- Per-customer/org breakdown in the default dashboard (Dedicated customers may require private metrics routing).
- Unbounded per-request dimensions (prompt hash, request id, user id, etc.).

---

### Required dimensions (tags)
All latency and first-token timing metrics MUST include the following tags:
- `model_version` (string, e.g., `llama3.1-70b-instruct@2026-03-07`)
- `route_name` (string, e.g., `chat.completions`)
- `io_mode` (`streaming` | `blocking`)
- `prompt_len_bucket` (token-based buckets; see below)
- `kv_cache_hit` (`true` | `false` | `unknown`)

- `client_region` (coarse: `na`, `eu`, `apac`, `sa`, `unknown`)
- `request_shape` (coarse: `short`, `medium`, `long`, `unknown`)

- `short`: `<128`

evidence.text:
description:
Problem: High-density dashboard views and canvased charts can overflow, clip awkwardly, or produce inconsistent stacking across Chromium, WebKit, and Firefox when viewport width is reduced and modals open. This causes visual artifacts (half-pixel strokes, shadow cutoffs), keyboard focus traps to break, and interactive table rows to become hard to target on touch devices. Goal: define compact-collapse heuristics for panels, standardized canvas clipping rules for charts and embeddable canvases, and a layering/z-index guardrail for modals/tooltips that behaves consistently across browsers and input modes. Deliver a set of prototypes, handoff-ready specs, and measurable acceptance criteria for engineering to implement in runtime-1.19/console-2026.03.

design_decisions:
Use semantic collapse tiers (primary/secondary) instead of purely pixel-driven shrinking to preserve core info density
Prefer CSS transform + overflow:hidden for canvas containers to avoid layout thrashing and preserve GPU compositing on Safari
Introduce a 10-level z-index scale (base, panel, overlay, modal, modal-top, toast) and require engineering to expose it as CSS tokens
Avoid CSS calc() reliance for critical clipping; instead provide explicit pixel fallbacks for older WebKit engines
Tooltips should render in a dedicated overlay root to avoid stacking context collisions with transformed parent nodes

acceptance_criteria:
Dense dashboard rows collapse to a predictable 2-tier distribution (primary/secondary) under 960px with no content overlap
Canvas-based charts render consistent axis hairlines and shadows across Chrome, Safari, and Firefox at devicePixelRatio 1 and 2
Modal stacking and tooltip z-order follow a deterministic rule set; keyboard focus trap and aria-hidden toggles work when multiple overlays are present
Touch hit targets for table rows and inline controls meet 44px minimum after density adjustments
Prototype validated in Chrome 116+, Safari 16+, Firefox 116+ with documented browser-specific workarounds

Figma prototype (compact + expanded states) with annotated constraints and responsive breakpoints
Interactive CodePen shim demonstrating canvas clip & shadow fixes
Handoff spec PDF with CSS variables, recommended z-index scale, and JS heuristics for collapse thresholds
Acceptance test checklist and cross-browser validation matrix

description:
Problem:
- High-density time-series (50k+ points) create heavy DOM and long paint times. Screen reader users get no concise context (raw axis values and long tables are noisy).
- We need a pattern in the design system that: 1) provides accessible, human-focused summaries of trends/anomalies; 2) reduces DOM/ARIA verbosity; 3) keeps interactive pan/zoom and tooltip fidelity for sighted users; 4) degrades gracefully on low-power devices.

Proposal:
- Condensed Narrative Mode (CNM): an optional chart mode that exposes a single accessible summary block per chart containing a short natural-language description (3-5 sentences) describing the dominant trend, latest value delta, detected anomalies (count + timestamps), and recommended follow-ups. The block is the primary screen-reader target (aria-live polite) instead of exposing every data point.
- Narrative templates: small, testable templates that cover monotonic trends, seasonal patterns, spikes/plateaus, and flatness. Maintain a templating spec in docs for consistency across charts.
- Hybrid Rendering Strategy: default visible layer uses decimated canvas drawing for the full series (fast paint, minimal DOM). An overlay SVG layer renders focus elements (selection handles, legend markers, hover lines) for crisp interaction and accessibility hooks (ARIA roles on handles, not on thousands of points).
- Keyboard / Focus model: keyboard focus lands on chart container -> control menu -> condensed narrative -> press Enter to toggle focus to interactive overlay (small number of interactive elements only).
- Energy and low-power mode: auto-enable more aggressive decimation on devices reporting reduced power mode or when battery low to preserve responsiveness.

- Accessibility:

evidence.title: Unified authorizer: core policy evaluator + authorization middleware for API, runtime, and console
evidence.text:
description:
Build RBAC v2 core: a centralized policy evaluation engine plus pluggable authorization middleware to enforce access across the Redwood API (hosted), serving runtime, and Redwood Console. Goals: 1) single consistent policy model and evaluation semantics for API endpoints, runtime token checks, and console UI; 2) native hooks for audit logging and traceability; 3) SSO/SAML and SCIM group-to-role bindings; 4) predictable performance for runtime path (low-latency checks) via fast cache and pre-evaluated bindings; 5) safe migration path from RBAC v1 with feature-flagged rollout and admin controls in Console.

design_decisions:
Policy language: adopt a compact JSON/YAML-based policy schema with CEL expressions for conditions (CEL chosen over Rego for smaller runtime and easier integration with Go services)
Deny-by-default: any unknown resource/action combination results in deny unless an allow policy explicitly matches
Evaluation side-effects: policies must be pure expressions; no side-effects allowed; audit hooks are separate and non-mutating
Sync vs async: API and Console checks are synchronous; runtime token check path uses a hot cache and optional async background refresh for slightly stale bindings
Cache strategy: LRU cache keyed by (principal, resource-type, action) with TTL configurable per deployment; default 30s for runtime, 5s for API gateway
Failure modes: when policy engine is unreachable, fallback policy is configurable per customer: 'fail-closed' for high-security customers, 'fail-open' for low-risk beta customers
SSO mapping: SAML group claims + SCIM provisioning map to role bindings in RBAC v2; mapping rules stored as part of org configuration and evaluated at login and token mint
Admin controls: Console exposes role editor, binding viewer, and audit log filters; destructive role edits require 2-step confirmation and are recorded in audit stream
Migration: RBAC v1 compatibility layer will translate v1 roles into equivalent v2 policies; migration completed per-org with a dry-run mode that logs mismatches
Observability: emit evaluation latency, cache hit/miss, policy compile errors, and per-tenant denied-count metrics to Console dashboards

implementation_plan:
1) Design doc + API contract (Confluence) -> https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/Sec/RBAC+v2+Policy+Engine
2) Core evaluator library in Go (pkg/authorizer) with CEL support; unit tests and fuzz tests
3) API gateway middleware (rest/authorizer) that uses the library and attaches audit events
4) Runtime integration: token-level check hook in serving runtime with optimized in-memory cache and per-GPU node process-local evaluator
5) Console UI: role/binding editor and admin change workflow; integration tests for UI + API
6) Migration tooling: v1->v2 translator and dry-run reporting endpoint
7) End-to-end e2e tests and canary rollout via feature flag 'rbac_v2_enabled'
Implementation PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/repo/pull/1234 (core evaluator), https://github

evidence.title: GPU BIOS & Firmware Orchestration — IaC Spec and Runbook
evidence.text:
OVERVIEW:

This page defines the specification, Terraform/IaC contracts, CI/CD pipeline, monitoring, and on-call runbook for coordinated BIOS and firmware updates on Redwood GPU fleet nodes. BIOS and base firmware updates are high-risk operations that can affect node bootability, driver compatibility, and inference SLOs; this doc codifies a safe, repeatable process tied to IaC metadata so updates are auditable, reversible, and can be phased across accounts/regions.

Audience and scope:
- Primary: eng-infra, eng-sre, eng-serving-runtime.
- Scope: Fleet-owned GPU hosts (bare-metal and cloud VM accelerators) under Redwood management; NOT customer-managed Private nodes.
- Excludes OS kernel/security patching workflows (covered in infra-image-rotation).

Goals and design principles:
- Safety-first: every update must provide an automated rollback path and pre-flight validation.
- Declarative metadata: firmware versions and desired BIOS configurations are expressed via Terraform variables and tag-based selectors.
- Minimal blast radius: phased canaries by topology (AZ, rack, instance-family).
- Observability: telemetry and automated health checks detect boot regressions within 10 minutes of update.
- Traceability: updates are recorded with audit metadata (operator, changelist, checksum).

Key concepts and terminology:
- Update Bundle: signed archive containing firmware binaries, vendor tooling, and a manifest (sha256 checksums + supported kernel/driver matrix).
- Node Selector: tag expression used by the provisioner to choose nodes (e.g., account:gpu-prod && instance-profile:a100-80g && rack:us-west-2a-row3).
- Drift Tag: fleet tag applied to nodes that have diverged from desired firmware (redwood:firmware_state=drift).
- Safe Mode Boot: a temporary boot configuration that prevents multi-GPU drivers from initializing; used for rollback validation when supported.

IaC / Terraform contract (module summary):
- Module name: redwood_gpu_firmware_operator
- Purpose: register an Update Bundle, define target selectors, and create a controlled run record for the orchestration pipeline.
- High-level variables (table):
| variable | type | description | example |
|----------|------|-------------|---------|
| name | string | human id for the update | "nv-bios-2026q1-a100" |
| bundle_s3_uri | string | signed bundle archive location | "s3://redwood-firmware/nv/2026q1.tar.gz" |
| checksum | string | sha256 of bundle | "abcdef..." |
| node_selector | string | terraform tag expression (see examples) | "account == 'gpu-prod' && family == 'a100-80g'" |
| canary_fraction | string | fractional canary (0.0 - 1.0) | "0.02" |
| maintenance_window | string | UTC cron window for apply | "Mon-Fri 01:00-04:00" |
| preflight_playbook_id | string | id of validation job (CI) | "firmware-preflight-42" |
| owner | string | primary owner/team | "eng-infra" |

  - run_id: unique orchestration run id (string)
  - bundle_manifest: artifact metadata reference

evidence.title: Webhook signature mismatch after client-side retry causes duplicated function-call side effects
evidence.text:
description:
Issue summary:
Customer BrightCart reports duplicated downstream side effects from function-calls triggered via Redwood streaming API. The customer observed that when their edge worker (Cloudflare) hits a transient timeout while processing our function-call callback, Redwood retries delivery. However, the first callback was received by BrightCart but the webhook verification signature they compute (HMAC-SHA256 of the canonicalized body) does not match the signature header in our retry request. As a result their endpoint returns 4xx for the retry while accepting the original, and they see duplicate processing of the same business action (order confirmation webhooks).

Impact:
- Duplicate order confirmations observed for ~0.3% of calls from the BrightCart integration over the last 24h (~120 duplicates).
- Customer is enterprise and reports these duplicates trigger payment reconciliation issues and manual support overhead.

Observed behavior:
- Initial callback arrives and is accepted (200). Shortly after, a retry from Redwood is sent (due to an intermediate timeout at customer's edge). The retry contains the same payload but the signature header (x-rw-signature) differs. BrightCart's verification rejects this retry (401) and their application performs a compensating re-processing that results in duplicate side effects.

Expected behavior:
- Retries should be byte-for-byte identical or signatures should verify equivalently after any transport changes. If any canonicalization occurs (gzip, newline normalization), we should surface that or avoid signing the body in a way that changes between attempts.

Key customer details and integration notes:
- BrightCart deployed a Cloudflare Worker that forwards the webhook to their internal API. The worker does minimal processing but performs an auto-decompression step in some fast-paths.
- They use our JS SDK (streaming + funcall callbacks).
- Their verification computes HMAC on the canonical JSON: compacted keys, 
  but it expects incoming body to match exactly what was signed earlier by Redwood's callback flow.

Attachments (provided by customer):
- Example successful callback (raw body and x-rw-signature header).
- Example retry that failed verification (raw body and x-rw-signature header).
- Cloudflare edge logs showing the timing and a transient 504 between their worker and origin roughly coincident with the retry window.

Steps to reproduce (approx):
1) Create a streaming session that triggers a function-call to BrightCart's webhook endpoint.
2) At the edge (simulate Cloudflare), force origin-to-worker request to experience a small timeout (drop the ACK) so Redwood considers delivery not confirmed and triggers retry path.
3) Inspect first and subsequent delivery bodies and x-rw-signature headers.

evidence.text:
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports duplicate downstream tool executions when a long-lived streaming request is retried after an OAuth token refresh. The customer uses our streaming SDK (Python) with an external webhook sink that verifies HMAC signatures (header: X-RW-SIG).

Impact:
- Duplicate external operations (billing webhooks, downstream provisioning) observed intermittently for ~3 customers on Dedicated tier.
- Reproducible under load with stream migration / region failover.

Environment:
- Dedicated tenant (TellusFin) running prod in us-east with secondary eu-west failover.
- SDKs: python 1.12.3, go 1.12.0 (edge), ts 1.11.7.

Steps to reproduce (from customer):
1) Open streaming function call with functions/toolchain enabled and a callback URL that validates HMAC signature (X-RW-SIG).
2) Simulate long-running generation (20-40s) and induce an OAuth refresh on client side by forcing token expiry mid-stream.
3) Cause a short network interruption (5s) or trigger region failover.
4) SDK reconnects, performs retry; callback is replayed but the downstream service sometimes treats it as a new invocation and performs the action again.

Observed behavior:
- Downstream verifies signature but intermittently rejects because signature encoding differs (base64 vs base64url and padding differences). When rejection occurs client retries, but idempotency-key header is sometimes rotated/truncated during the SDK's token refresh code path, so server receives what looks like a fresh invocation.
- Platform logs show the original tool invocation completed but the retry was accepted and executed again, producing duplicate side effects.

Expected behavior:
- Retries should be deduplicated by idempotency key regardless of token refresh. Signature encoding normalization should not cause valid retries to be treated as new requests.

Attachments / sample logs provided by customer (redacted):
- request headers (orig): X-RW-SIG: HMAC-SHA256 base64=QmFzZTY0UGFkZGVk...
- request headers (retry after refresh): X-RW-SIG: HMAC-SHA256 base64url=QmFzZTY0UGFkZGVk (no padding)
- idempotency-key sometimes shows suffix ":refresh" on retry in python-sdk logs.
- Correlated platform trace: trace_id=tr_0a3f... shows two completions for tool-run id tr_0a3f-run-12

SRE (Ben): Initial hypothesis: SDK retry logic replays the function call because we only consider final success when function execution completes. If callback returns 202 (accepted), we treat that as success upstream but the streaming retry path may re-emit before the ACK is fully recorded in our request-state store.
Customer (DocuLend Engineer): We rely on 202 because jobs are enqueued for long-running processing. Our webhook cannot synchronously confirm completion. How should we deduplicate from our side?
Support (Aisha): Short-term workaround: include a client-generated idempotency token in function_call arguments yourself (e.g., job_client_id) and dedupe on webhook side. We'll follow up with engineering on server-side guards.
Eng (Ben): Creating follow-ups to evaluate persisting function-call ACKs earlier in the pipeline and to add a recommended SDK helper for attaching a per-function idempotency header. See linked PR that prototypes an option: https://github.com/redwood-inference/platform/pull/4821

investigation_notes:
Reproduced in prod-like dedicated pool with synthetic load (test customer account).
Tracing shows two distinct server-side function-call events emitted with two different internal event ids; both were delivered to webhook because webhook ACK was 202 and we did not mark the call as 'durably recorded' until later in the pipeline.
Root cause hypothesis: race between streaming connection retry path and durable write of function-call metadata to the event-store. When reconnect/retry occurs before durable write completes, the request is replayed and results in a duplicate downstream invocation.

Northpeak Search’s higher‑than‑expected Dedicated Burst Usage was caused by a bug that double‑counted burst metering for requests that were retried. evidence.text:
Overview

Purpose: This document defines the first-responder responsibilities, an availability matrix for responder coverage, escalation heuristics, and ready-to-use communication templates for customer-facing status updates and internal bridge notes. It is intended for on-call engineers, SREs, support, and incident commanders.

Scope: Applies to all Redwood Inference production services (examples: redwood-api, redwood-serving, control-plane, kv-cache, routing-proxy). Does not replace existing service-specific runbooks; it complements them with standard response patterns and message templates.

1) Responder availability matrix (how to interpret coverage)

Columns: Role | Primary responsibility | Typical page window | Expected ack | Typical handoff
- Primary on-call: Service triage, mitigation, short-term remediation | 24x7 | 5 minutes | Handoff to secondary or platform after 2 hours
- Secondary on-call: Tier-2 escalation, deep-dive assistance, cross-service coordination | business hours + weekends followups | 30 minutes | Take ownership if primary unavailable for >30m
- Platform SRE: Capacity/fleet & region failover | business hours with on-call rotation | 60 minutes | Coordinate region failover actions
- Incident Commander (IC): Incident lifecycle & stakeholder comms | invoked as needed | 15 minutes | Own incident timeline until postmortem

Availability rules (operationalized):
- Pager windows and contactable status must be reflected in the oncall roster and Slack presence flags.
- If a primary on-call does not ack within expected ack time, the pager policy escalates to secondary, then to IC escalation roster.

2) Severity definitions and primary actions (quick reference)

- Sev0 (Critical outage; customer-impacting, no viable fallback):
  - Target ack: 2 minutes.
  - Actions: Immediate bridge (Zoom/Jabber), route traffic to fallback region/model variant if possible, engage IC, notify GTM/CS for customer-impact comms.
  - Escalation window: 5 minutes to engage leadership.

- Sev1 (Major degradation; significant error rate or latency regression affecting many customers):
  - Target ack: 5 minutes.
  - Actions: Open bridge, start triage (service logs, SLO dashboards, recent deploys), enable circuit-breakers or rate-limits, begin customer status draft.

- Sev2 (Partial degradation; single region or small customer subset impacted):
  - Target ack: 15 minutes.
  - Actions: Triage with limited bridge, consider failover, prepare targeted customer comms if impact persists >1 hour.

- Sev3 (Non-urgent; operational issue with no immediate customer impact):
  - Target ack: 4 hours.
  - Actions: Create a ticket, assign owner, schedule remediation in next sprint.

3) Escalation heuristics (decision ladder)

1. Detect & verify: Confirm alert validity (noise reduction) using dashboard checks and log sampling.
2. Contain & stabilize: If possible, apply safe mitigations (temporary scaling, circuit-breakers, config rollback).
3. Communicate & coordinate: Stand up

evidence.title: Respond, Recover, Review: Incident Playbook and Game Day Syllabus
evidence.text:
Overview

Purpose: This document describes a single, opinionated lifecycle for incidents at Redwood: Respond → Recover → Review. It consolidates triage ladders, step-by-step containment and recovery runbooks, a postmortem template, on-call rotation rules, and a reproducible game day syllabus for team readiness. Use this as the canonical operational path for any incident affecting customer-facing inference services or control plane components.

Scope
- Applies to all production incidents impacting Redwood-hosted API, Dedicated capacity, and Private control plane services.
- Excludes non-prod test environments (see team wiki for staging incident guidance).

Quick definitions
- Incident: any event causing customer-visible degradation, increased error rates, latency SLO breaches, or data integrity issues.
- Major incident: multi-region outage, sustained latency SLO violations >30m, or data loss.
- Bridge: primary coordination channel (Slack #inc-bridge by default).

Roles & ownership
1) Incident Commander (IC): owns triage decisions, public comms, and rollback choices. Usually senior SRE or on-call service owner.
2) Bridge Operator: runs the bridge, collects evidence, and creates updates. Typically the on-call SRE.
3) Subject Matter Experts (SMEs): runtime, networking, database, billing, security.
4) Customer Liaison: customer-success engineer for customer-impacted incidents.
5) Postmortem Author: the person who documents the timeline and actions within 72 hours.

Triage decision ladder (first 15 minutes)
1) Detect: alert fires or customer report.
2) Acknowledge: on-call sets initial status in the bridge within 5 minutes.
3) Classify: apply the impact matrix (below) and decide major vs minor.
4) IC assignment: if major, escalate to IC immediately; if minor, on-call handles.
5) Stabilize: execute containment runbook snippets.

Impact matrix (short)
| Customer Impact | Traffic impact | SLO impact | Classification |
|-----------------|----------------|------------|----------------|
| Single customer, degraded responses | <1% traffic | None/very small | P2 |
| Multiple customers, increased latency | 1-10% traffic | SLO at risk | P1 |
| Widespread errors or region down | >10% | SLO breach | Major/P0 |

Immediate containment runbook (first 30 minutes)
1) Put a short-status placeholder: "Investigation underway; initial mitigation in progress."
2) Turn off automated scaling/burst if it's causing churn (CLI: redwood infra scale --service <svc> --mode paused).
3) Apply quick-filters: route new traffic to fallback model variant or healthy region per routing policy. Example: set routing policy via console -> Traffic -> Fallback: small-model-v1.
4) If CPU/GPU exhaustion: evict long-running jobs and enable preemptible fallback pools. Command sample: kubectl cordon <node> && redwood node-drain --evict-long-kv --force.
5) If memory leakage suspected: restart the service with crash-loop protection removed: systemctl restart redwood-runtime-<svc> or k roll restart <de
